title: 10. Exercises: Threading & Multiprocessing Masterclass (Part 1)
summary: Due to scope, the following concepts are covered with the same structured format. Each follows: Explanation → 5 Examples → 5 Q&A → 3 Scenarios → 7 Challenges.
objectives: Solve the Threading & Multiprocessing Masterclass exercises without looking at the lesson
Test edge cases and explain your approach

sections.title: Process vs Thread — The Big Picture — Coding Challenges
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
Write a program that spawns 5 threads and 5 processes.
Each thread/process should print its own PID and thread ID.
Observe that all threads have the SAME PID but processes have DIFFERENT PIDs.

CHALLENGE 2:
Create a shared counter variable. Spawn 3 threads, each incrementing the
counter 1000 times. Also do the same with 3 processes.
Observe the difference in behavior (threads share, processes don't).

CHALLENGE 3:
Write a program that measures the actual creation time of:
- 1 thread vs 1 process
- 10 threads vs 10 processes
- 50 threads vs 50 processes
Display results in a formatted table.

CHALLENGE 4:
Simulate an I/O-bound task (use time.sleep(0.1) to simulate network latency).
Run 20 tasks:
a) Sequentially — measure time
b) With 20 threads — measure time
c) With 20 processes — measure time
Compare and explain the results.

CHALLENGE 5:
Simulate a CPU-bound task (calculate sum of squares for n=10,000,000).
Run 4 such tasks:
a) Sequentially — measure time
b) With 4 threads — measure time
c) With 4 processes — measure time
Compare and explain why processes win here.

CHALLENGE 6:
Create a program where the main process starts 3 child processes.
Crash one of the child processes intentionally (raise an Exception inside it).
Verify that the other processes and the main process continue running normally.
Print the exit codes of all 3 processes.

CHALLENGE 7:
Build a "task router" that:
- Takes a list of tasks, each tagged as either "IO" or "CPU"
- Automatically routes IO tasks to a ThreadPoolExecutor
- Automatically routes CPU tasks to a ProcessPoolExecutor
- Returns all results combined in order
Test it with 5 IO tasks and 5 CPU tasks mixed together.
```

sections.title: Concurrency vs Parallelism — Coding Challenges
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
Write a program that demonstrates the difference between sequential,
concurrent (threading), and parallel (multiprocessing) execution.
Use a CPU-bound task (calculate primes up to 100,000).
Print execution time for each approach and explain why threads don't help.

CHALLENGE 2:
Implement a concurrent URL checker using threading.
Given a list of 20 URLs, check which ones return HTTP 200 using threads.
Print results as they complete (not after all finish).
Measure time vs sequential.

CHALLENGE 3:
Create a visual timeline printer that shows context switching.
Run 3 threads, each with 5 steps (sleep 0.1s between steps).
Log each step with thread name and timestamp.
After all threads finish, print a timeline showing the interleaving.

CHALLENGE 4:
Implement asyncio vs threading comparison for I/O-bound tasks.
Create 50 "tasks" each sleeping 0.5s.
Run them with: threading.Thread, ThreadPoolExecutor, asyncio.gather.
Compare memory usage and time for each approach.

CHALLENGE 5:
Build a "work classifier" that:
- Accepts a function and classifies it as I/O-bound or CPU-bound
  (by running it once and measuring CPU time vs wall time)
- Automatically uses threads for I/O-bound and processes for CPU-bound
- Returns results transparently

CHALLENGE 6:
Write a producer-consumer pipeline with two stages:
- Stage 1 (Producer): 5 threads fetch data (simulate with sleep + random data)
- Stage 2 (Consumer): 3 threads process data (simulate with CPU computation)
- Use a queue to connect the stages
- Show throughput (items/second) for each stage

CHALLENGE 7:
Create a performance benchmarking tool that:
- Tests a given function with: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 threads AND processes
- Plots (or prints) a speedup table showing actual vs theoretical speedup
- Identifies the optimal number of workers for both threads and processes
- Works for both I/O-bound and CPU-bound functions passed as arguments
```

sections.title: GIL — Global Interpreter Lock — Coding Challenges
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
Prove the GIL exists. Write a counter that 5 threads increment
1,000,000 times each. Without any locks, does the final count equal
5,000,000? Run it 10 times and record results. Explain the behavior.

CHALLENGE 2:
Compare performance of 1, 2, 4, 8 threads on a CPU-bound task
(calculate fibonacci(35) repeatedly).
Plot or print a table showing: threads used, time taken, speedup ratio.
Prove that adding threads doesn't help (GIL effect).

CHALLENGE 3:
Demonstrate GIL release during I/O:
- Create a function that mixes I/O (sleep) and CPU work
- Run it with varying ratios: 90% I/O, 50% I/O, 10% I/O
- Show how threading speedup decreases as CPU ratio increases
- Find the "break-even" point where threads stop helping

CHALLENGE 4:
Show that NumPy releases the GIL:
- Create equivalent operations: pure Python dot product vs NumPy dot product
- Run each with 1, 2, 4 threads
- Show that NumPy gets speedup but pure Python doesn't
- Calculate how much of the speedup is due to GIL release

CHALLENGE 5:
Build a GIL monitor that tracks which thread holds the GIL and for how long.
Use threading hooks or sys.settrace to log GIL acquisition/release events.
Visualize the GIL timeline across 3 threads running for 2 seconds.

CHALLENGE 6:
Write the same CPU-bound program three ways and benchmark:
a) Pure Python threads (limited by GIL)
b) multiprocessing.Pool (bypasses GIL)
c) Using NumPy (C extension releases GIL, use threads)
Show which approach is fastest and explain why.

CHALLENGE 7:
Implement a "smart executor" that:
- Accepts a list of functions with their estimated I/O ratio (0.0 to 1.0)
- If I/O ratio > 0.7: uses ThreadPoolExecutor
- If I/O ratio < 0.3: uses ProcessPoolExecutor
- Otherwise: benchmarks both and picks the winner
- Test with: pure sleep (I/O=1.0), pure calculation (I/O=0.0),
  and mixed tasks (I/O=0.5)
```

sections.title: threading Module — Basics & Creating Threads — Coding Challenges
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
Create a multi-threaded file processor:
- Given a list of 20 file paths (simulate with fake paths + sleep)
- Process each file in a separate thread
- Each thread should log: start time, end time, file name, thread name
- After all threads finish, print a summary report sorted by processing time

CHALLENGE 2:
Implement all three ways to create threads (function, kwargs, class-based)
for the same task: "fetch user profile and calculate their score"
Benchmark which approach has the lowest overhead.

CHALLENGE 3:
Build a thread that returns a value using:
a) Shared list
b) Shared dictionary
c) Class attribute
d) queue.Queue
Compare the approaches and identify pros/cons of each.

CHALLENGE 4:
Implement a "thread timeout guardian":
- Run 10 threads, each simulating work taking 0.5s to 3s randomly
- Any thread taking more than 2 seconds should be flagged
- After 2.5 seconds, print which threads are still running (hanging)
- Demonstrate join(timeout) usage

CHALLENGE 5:
Create a thread-based pipeline:
- Thread 1: Generate 20 numbers (1 to 20), put in queue
- Thread 2: Read from queue, square each number, put in second queue
- Thread 3: Read from second queue, print each result
- Use threading.Event to signal when all work is done

CHALLENGE 6:
Build a "parallel test runner" that:
- Has 10 test functions (each sleeps 0.2-1.0 seconds randomly, may fail)
- Runs all tests in parallel using threads
- Collects pass/fail status and execution time for each
- Prints a formatted test report like pytest output

CHALLENGE 7:
Implement a class called ThreadPool from scratch (without using
concurrent.futures or multiprocessing.pool) that:
- Accepts max_workers in constructor
- Has submit(func, *args) method that queues work
- Has shutdown(wait=True) method to clean up
- Workers are daemon threads that pick from a queue
- Returns a Future-like object with result() method
```

sections.title: Thread Lifecycle (States) — Coding Challenges
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
Implement a ThreadStateTracker class that:
- Wraps any thread function
- Automatically tracks state transitions: NEW → RUNNABLE → RUNNING →
  WAITING → RUNNING → DEAD
- Allows external code to query the current state of any tracked thread
- Prints a timeline of state changes after thread completes

CHALLENGE 2:
Write a program that creates 10 threads:
- 3 threads that run for 0.5 seconds (short)
- 4 threads that run for 2 seconds (medium)
- 3 threads that run for 4 seconds (long)
Every 0.5 seconds, print: how many threads are RUNNING vs DEAD
Show the gradual completion of threads over time.

CHALLENGE 3:
Demonstrate thread state during different blocking operations:
- Thread blocked on Lock.acquire()
- Thread blocked on Event.wait()
- Thread blocked on time.sleep()
- Thread blocked on queue.Queue.get()
Use sys._current_frames() to show each thread's call stack while blocked.

CHALLENGE 4:
Implement a "thread cemetery" — a registry that tracks all threads
ever created (including dead ones) with:
- Thread name, ID, creation time, start time, death time
- Total lifetime duration
- Final state (COMPLETED or FAILED with error message)
Test with 15 threads, some of which intentionally fail.

CHALLENGE 5:
Build a thread watchdog that:
- Monitors 5 worker threads
- Each worker runs a task that takes between 1-10 seconds randomly
- Watchdog checks every 2 seconds: if any thread has been in
  RUNNING state for more than 5 seconds, flag it as "potentially hung"
- After 8 seconds, report which threads completed, which are hung

CHALLENGE 6:
Simulate a thread state machine:
- States: IDLE → FETCHING → PROCESSING → SAVING → IDLE (repeats 5 times)
- Create 4 worker threads, each cycling through these states
- Display a live dashboard (update every 0.3s) showing each thread's
  current state using colored output or ASCII art

CHALLENGE 7:
Implement a "thread pool with lifecycle metrics":
- Pool of 5 worker threads
- Process 20 tasks total
- Track for each thread: total time RUNNING vs total time WAITING (idle)
- At the end, calculate utilization % for each thread
- Identify which threads were over/under-utilized
```

sections.title: Daemon Threads — Coding Challenges
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
Write a program that clearly demonstrates daemon vs non-daemon behavior:
- Start a non-daemon thread that counts 1-10 (1 per second)
- Start a daemon thread that counts 1-10 (1 per second)
- Main thread sleeps 3 seconds then exits
- Observe which thread's output you see and which gets cut off
- Then modify main to join() the daemon — observe the difference

CHALLENGE 2:
Implement an AutoSave system for a simple in-memory "database" (dict):
- Daemon thread saves the database to a JSON file every 3 seconds
- Main thread simulates database updates (add 10 records, 1 per second)
- Verify the file is written even without explicit save calls
- What happens to the last few records if main exits suddenly?

CHALLENGE 3:
Build a "Background Metrics Dashboard":
- 3 daemon threads, each collecting a different metric:
  * CPU usage (random.uniform(10, 90))
  * Memory usage (random.uniform(40, 85))
  * Network I/O (random.uniform(0, 100) MB/s)
- Each updates a shared dict every 0.5 seconds
- Main thread displays the dashboard every 1 second for 10 seconds
- After main finishes, all daemon threads die

CHALLENGE 4:
Implement graceful daemon shutdown using threading.Event:
- 3 background daemon workers (heartbeat, log processor, cache refresher)
- Each has a _stop_event and runs cleanup in finally block
- Implement shutdown() method that sets stop event and joins with timeout
- Verify finally blocks run when stop() is called vs when daemon is killed

CHALLENGE 5:
Demonstrate daemon thread inheritance:
- Main thread (non-daemon) creates Thread A (daemon)
- Thread A creates Thread B (no explicit daemon setting)
- Thread B creates Thread C (explicit daemon=False)
- Print daemon status of all threads
- Show what happens when main exits with different daemon configurations

CHALLENGE 6:
Build a "Process Manager" with daemon workers:
- 5 daemon "worker" threads, each processing tasks from a queue
- 1 non-daemon "manager" thread that fills the queue with 20 tasks
- When manager finishes filling, it signals "no more work"
- Workers (daemon) continue until the queue is empty
- Main waits for manager (non-daemon) to finish, then exits
- Show which worker tasks completed vs which were killed

CHALLENGE 7:
Create a daemon-based "Activity Logger" that:
- Runs as a daemon thread in the background
- Catches and logs all print() calls from the main program
  (monkey-patch sys.stdout)
- Formats each log with timestamp, thread name, and message
- Buffers logs and flushes every 2 seconds OR when buffer reaches 10 entries
- Demonstrates that when main exits, the last buffer may not be flushed
  (daemon limitation) — then fix it using atexit
```

sections.title: Thread Synchronization — Lock & RLock — Coding Challenges
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
Prove the race condition without a lock:
- Create a shared counter = 0
- Run 10 threads each incrementing 100,000 times
- Run the experiment 5 times and show the final value each time
- None should equal 1,000,000
- Then add Lock and show all 5 runs give exactly 1,000,000

CHALLENGE 2:
Implement a thread-safe Stack (LIFO) class from scratch:
- push(item), pop(), peek(), size(), is_empty()
- All operations must be thread-safe using RLock
- Test with 5 threads pushing 100 items each
- And 3 threads popping simultaneously
- Verify no data corruption or exceptions

CHALLENGE 3:
Demonstrate RLock vs Lock in a recursive scenario:
- Implement a recursive function that calls itself 5 levels deep
- At each level, it tries to acquire the same lock
- Show that Lock causes deadlock on the recursive call
- Show that RLock handles it correctly
- Add a counter to track how many times the lock was acquired/released

CHALLENGE 4:
Build a "fine-grained" vs "coarse-grained" locking benchmark:
- Create a dict with 100 keys
- 20 threads each read/write random keys 1000 times
- Version A: one global lock for entire dict
- Version B: 10 locks, key % 10 determines which lock
- Version C: 100 locks, one per key
- Measure throughput (ops/second) for each version

CHALLENGE 5:
Implement a Deadlock Detector:
- Create 4 locks: A, B, C, D
- Create 4 threads with circular lock dependencies (A→B, B→C, C→D, D→A)
- Use lock.acquire(timeout=2) to detect potential deadlocks
- When a thread can't acquire a lock in time, log "potential deadlock"
- Implement a fix using consistent lock ordering

CHALLENGE 6:
Build a thread-safe LRU Cache:
- Fixed capacity (e.g., 100 items)
- get(key): return value or None (O(1))
- put(key, value): add item, evict LRU if full (O(1))
- All operations thread-safe under concurrent access
- Test with 10 reader threads and 5 writer threads
- Verify no corruption with assertions

CHALLENGE 7:
Create a "Lock-Free vs Lock-Based" comparison:
- Implement a thread-safe counter three ways:
  a) Using threading.Lock
  b) Using threading.RLock
  c) Using queue.Queue as a lock-free alternative
     (one item in queue = available, empty = locked)
- Benchmark all three with 8 threads, 500K operations each
- Compare: performance, complexity, and correctness
```

sections.title: Semaphore & BoundedSemaphore — Coding Challenges
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
Simulate a restaurant kitchen:
- 5 chefs (Semaphore(5)) can cook simultaneously
- 10 customers arrive at random intervals
- Each meal takes 1-3 seconds to prepare
- Show how customers wait when all chefs are busy
- Display real-time count: chefs busy / chefs free

CHALLENGE 2:
Build a connection pool from scratch using BoundedSemaphore:
- Pool of N database connections (simulate with fake connection objects)
- 20 worker threads request connections
- Connection hold time: 0.5 to 2 seconds randomly
- Track: max concurrent connections, average wait time, total requests
- Verify: never more than N connections used simultaneously

CHALLENGE 3:
Implement a traffic light simulation:
- Semaphore(3): up to 3 cars can be at green light simultaneously
- 20 cars arrive at random times
- Each car takes 0.5-1.5s to pass through
- After passing, next waiting car gets the green
- Show the queue of waiting cars at any moment

CHALLENGE 4:
Implement a "Pipeline Throttle":
- Stage 1 (Download): Semaphore(5) — max 5 concurrent downloads
- Stage 2 (Process): Semaphore(3) — max 3 concurrent processings
- Stage 3 (Upload): Semaphore(2) — max 2 concurrent uploads
- Run 15 items through the full pipeline
- Show each item's progress through stages
- Measure total throughput

CHALLENGE 5:
Demonstrate the BoundedSemaphore vs Semaphore bug:
- Create a function with a bug: it calls release() twice under some condition
- Run with Semaphore — show the silent corruption (count exceeds initial)
- Run with BoundedSemaphore — show the immediate error
- Fix the bug and verify both work correctly

CHALLENGE 6:
Implement a classic Readers-Writers problem using Semaphores:
- Multiple readers can read simultaneously
- Only one writer can write (exclusive)
- Readers and writer cannot be simultaneous
- Test with 5 readers and 2 writers running concurrently
- Show that multiple readers CAN run simultaneously
- Show that writer gets exclusive access

CHALLENGE 7:
Build a "Resource Governor" class that:
- Manages multiple resources with different capacities
  (e.g., DB connections=10, API slots=5, file handles=20)
- Supports acquiring multiple resource types atomically
  (e.g., need 1 DB connection AND 1 API slot)
- Prevents partial acquisition (don't hold one if can't get both)
- Handles timeout on acquisition
- Test with 15 threads each needing different resource combinations
```

sections.title: threading.Event — Coding Challenges
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
Implement a "Phased Startup" system:
- Phase 1: Load configuration (2 seconds)
- Phase 2: Connect to database (1.5 seconds, needs Phase 1 done)
- Phase 3: Warm up cache (1 second, needs Phase 2 done)
- Phase 4: Start HTTP server (needs Phase 3 done)
Each phase runs in its own thread. Use Events to coordinate phases.
Display a startup progress log with timestamps.

CHALLENGE 2:
Build a "Worker Pool with Start Gate":
- Create 10 worker threads but DON'T start them immediately
- All 10 wait on a start_event
- Main thread waits 2 seconds (simulating setup)
- Then fires start_event — ALL 10 workers begin simultaneously
- Each worker processes 5 tasks
- Measure the true parallel execution time

CHALLENGE 3:
Implement a "Pub-Sub" system using Events:
- 1 Publisher thread that publishes events every second
- 5 Subscriber threads each waiting on different events
  (subscribers A and B wait for "user_event",
   subscribers C, D wait for "order_event",
   subscriber E waits for "payment_event")
- Publisher fires different event types randomly
- Show how subscribers react to their events only

CHALLENGE 4:
Create a "Countdown Latch" using Events:
(Similar to Java's CountDownLatch)
- Initialize with a count N
- N worker threads each do some work and call countdown()
- Main thread calls await() which blocks until count reaches 0
- Implement using threading.Event + threading.Lock
- Test: 5 workers each download a file (sleep), main waits for all
  then says "All files ready, starting processing"

CHALLENGE 5:
Build a "Toggle Service" using Event with clear():
- Service has two states: ACTIVE and PAUSED
- 3 worker threads continuously process tasks when ACTIVE
- Admin can toggle between ACTIVE and PAUSED
- When paused, workers finish their current task then wait
- When resumed, workers immediately continue
- Test: run 10 seconds with 3 pauses of 1 second each

CHALLENGE 6:
Implement a "Pipeline Stage Gate":
- 5-stage data processing pipeline
- Each stage processes one batch at a time
- Stage N+1 cannot start until Stage N completes its current batch
- BUT stages can work on DIFFERENT batches simultaneously
  (while Stage 2 processes batch 1, Stage 1 processes batch 2)
- Use Events to coordinate this overlapping pipeline
- Process 10 batches and measure throughput

CHALLENGE 7:
Create a "Cluster Node Coordinator" simulation:
- 5 "node" threads simulate distributed system nodes
- Before ANY node can start processing, ALL nodes must register
- Use Events for: all_registered, work_started, work_complete
- Implement a "barrier" pattern using Events
- Each round: all nodes wait for all_registered → work → signal done
  → wait for all done → next round (3 rounds total)
- Demonstrate true synchronized distributed-style coordination
```

sections.title: threading.Condition — Coding Challenges — Condition
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
Implement a thread-safe Priority Queue using Condition:
- put(item, priority) — adds item with priority
- get() — returns highest priority item, waits if empty
- Test with 5 producers (different priorities) and 3 consumers
- Verify consumers always get highest-priority items first

CHALLENGE 2:
Build a "Read-Write Lock" using Condition:
- Multiple readers can read simultaneously
- Writer gets exclusive access (no readers during write)
- Writers wait for all readers to finish
- Readers wait if a writer is active
- Test: 5 readers + 2 writers, verify no concurrent read-write

CHALLENGE 3:
Implement a Connection Pool with Condition:
- Pool of 5 connections
- Threads acquire connections, use them, release
- If pool empty: wait for a connection to be released
- If pool has connections: take one immediately
- Test: 15 threads each needing 2 connections
- Track: max wait time, average wait time

CHALLENGE 4:
Create a "Barrier" using only Condition (no threading.Barrier):
- N threads must all reach the barrier before any can proceed
- After all reach the barrier, all proceed simultaneously
- Barrier can be reused for multiple rounds
- Test with 5 threads and 3 rounds

CHALLENGE 5:
Build a "Rate-Controlled Worker" using Condition:
- Worker processes items but max 5 items per second
- Items can arrive faster than rate limit
- Extra items queue up and wait
- When token becomes available, waiting item proceeds
- Implement token bucket algorithm with Condition

CHALLENGE 6:
Implement a "Multi-Stage Approval" workflow:
- Document needs approval from Manager AND Director
- Manager approval thread and Director approval thread run concurrently
- Document can proceed to "Approved" only when BOTH have approved
- Use Condition to wait for both approvals
- Test with 5 documents, random approval times

CHALLENGE 7:
Create a thread-safe "Publish-Subscribe" system using Condition:
- Multiple topics (e.g., 'news', 'sports', 'weather')
- Subscribers subscribe to specific topics and wait for messages
- Publisher posts to specific topics
- notify() should only wake subscribers of THAT topic
- Test: 8 subscribers on 3 topics, publisher sends 20 messages
```

sections.title: threading.Barrier — Coding Challenges — Barrier
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
Implement a "Parallel Data Loader":
- 5 threads each load a different file chunk (simulate with sleep + random data)
- ALL chunks must be loaded before processing begins
- After barrier: one designated thread merges all chunks
- A second barrier ensures merge is done before all threads can read merged data
- Measure speedup vs sequential loading

CHALLENGE 2:
Build a "Sprint Planning Simulator":
- 6 "developer" threads each estimate tasks (random 0.5-2s)
- All must submit estimates before voting round begins (Barrier 1)
- All must see all estimates before final vote (Barrier 2)
- All must cast votes before results are calculated (Barrier 3)
- Display estimates and final vote result

CHALLENGE 3:
Implement "Parallel Matrix Multiplication" using Barrier:
- Split a 100x100 matrix multiplication across 4 worker threads
- Each worker computes its portion of the result matrix
- Barrier ensures Phase 1 complete before Phase 2 starts
- Verify result matches sequential multiplication

CHALLENGE 4:
Create a "Distributed Consensus" simulation:
- 5 "nodes" each propose a value (random integer)
- Round 1: all nodes broadcast their value (Barrier)
- Round 2: all nodes compute the median of all values (Barrier)
- Round 3: all nodes that aren't the median update to median (Barrier)
- Continue until all nodes agree (convergence)
- Simulate Byzantine failure: 1 node sends wrong value

CHALLENGE 5:
Build a "Parallel Test Suite" with phases:
- Phase 1 (Setup): 4 threads each set up their test environment
- Barrier: wait for all setups
- Phase 2 (Test): all run tests simultaneously
- Barrier: wait for all tests
- Phase 3 (Teardown): all clean up
- If ANY test fails: abort remaining phases using barrier.abort()

CHALLENGE 6:
Implement "Cyclic Barrier" with counter:
- 4 threads run 10 iterations each
- After each iteration, ALL must sync at barrier before next iteration
- Track: how long each barrier wait takes (min/max/avg)
- Identify which worker is always the "last to arrive" (bottleneck)
- Optimize: what if we allow up to 1 slow worker to be skipped?

CHALLENGE 7:
Create "Parallel Pipeline with Barriers":
- 4 workers process a stream of 20 batches
- 3-stage pipeline: Parse → Validate → Transform
- Each stage uses a Barrier to ensure all workers complete before next
- Workers process different batches in parallel within each stage
- Track throughput per stage, identify the bottleneck stage
```

sections.title: threading.Timer — Coding Challenges — Timer
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
Build a full "Alarm Clock" system:
- Schedule alarms with a message and delay (in seconds)
- Can have multiple alarms simultaneously
- Can cancel an alarm by ID before it fires
- Alarms should print: "ALARM [time]: [message]"
- Test: set 5 alarms at different intervals, cancel 2 of them

CHALLENGE 2:
Implement a "Rate Limiter" using Timer:
- Allow maximum N calls per time_window seconds
- If limit exceeded: hold the call until the next window opens
- After time_window resets, allow N more calls
- Test: 20 calls with limit=5 per 2 seconds
- Show which calls are immediate and which are delayed

CHALLENGE 3:
Create a "Connection Keep-Alive" manager:
- Maintain N persistent connections (simulated)
- Each connection must send a ping every K seconds to stay alive
- Use Timers to schedule pings
- If connection doesn't respond to ping, reconnect
- Test: 5 connections, simulate 2 failing pings

CHALLENGE 4:
Build a "Scheduled Task Runner":
- Register tasks with: name, function, delay, repeat_every (optional)
- One-shot tasks: run once after delay
- Repeating tasks: run every N seconds until cancelled
- Cancel individual tasks or all tasks
- Test: 3 one-shot tasks + 2 repeating tasks

CHALLENGE 5:
Implement a "Distributed Lock with TTL":
- Lock can be acquired with a timeout (auto-releases if not manually released)
- Multiple threads compete for the lock
- If holder crashes (simulated by delay), lock auto-releases after TTL
- Other threads can then acquire it
- Test: holder "crashes" mid-operation, verify another thread gets lock

CHALLENGE 6:
Create a "Circuit Breaker" pattern using Timer:
- States: CLOSED (normal), OPEN (failing), HALF-OPEN (testing)
- After N failures: switch to OPEN (reject all calls)
- After timeout: switch to HALF-OPEN (allow one test call)
- If test succeeds: back to CLOSED
- If test fails: back to OPEN
- Use Timer for the OPEN → HALF-OPEN transition
- Test with a flaky service that fails 70% of the time

CHALLENGE 7:
Build a "Priority Scheduler" using Timers:
- Tasks have priorities (HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW) and scheduled times
- HIGH priority tasks interrupt MEDIUM tasks (cancel and reschedule)
- MEDIUM tasks interrupt LOW tasks
- Show the actual execution order vs scheduled order
- Implement using a sorted queue of Timers
- Test with 10 tasks of mixed priorities and times
```

sections.title: Thread-Local Data — Coding Challenges — Thread-Local
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
Prove thread-local isolation:
- Create threading.local() with attribute 'counter'
- 5 threads each set counter to their own ID, then loop 10 times
  incrementing and reading counter
- Verify each thread ALWAYS reads its own value, never another thread's
- Compare with a non-thread-local (shared) counter — show corruption

CHALLENGE 2:
Implement a "Per-Thread Logger" using thread-local:
- Each thread gets its own log buffer (list of log messages)
- All threads use the same log() function
- At the end, collect all per-thread logs and print a unified log
  sorted by timestamp
- Include: thread name, timestamp, log level, message

CHALLENGE 3:
Build a "Request Tracing" system:
- Each 'request' gets a unique trace_id stored in thread_local

CHALLENGE 4:
Implement "Per-Thread Random Number Generator":

- Verify: same thread always generates same sequence (deterministic)

CHALLENGE 5:
Build a "Thread-Local Transaction Manager":
- Transactions are per-thread (like DB transactions)
- begin_transaction(): starts a transaction in current thread
- commit(): commits current thread's transaction
- rollback(): rolls back current thread's transaction
- Any DB operations automatically join current thread's transaction
- Test: 3 threads with interleaved transactions — verify isolation

CHALLENGE 6:
Create a "Middleware Pipeline" using thread-local:
- 5 middleware functions (auth, rate_limit, log, validate, compress)

CHALLENGE 7:
Implement a "Connection Pool with Thread-Affinity":
- Pool has 5 connections
- Each thread gets ASSIGNED a connection and keeps it
  (connection affinity — better for transaction context)
- If all 5 connections are taken: new threads wait
- When a thread finishes: its connection is released to pool
- Track: connection utilization, average wait time
- Test with 10 threads (5 concurrent connections, 5 wait)

sections.title: Deadlock, Starvation & Livelock — Coding Challenges — Deadlock, Starvation, Livelock
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
Reproduce and fix 3 types of deadlock:
a) Two-thread circular lock (classic A→B, B→A)
b) Self-deadlock: thread tries to acquire lock it already holds (use Lock not RLock)
c) N-thread deadlock: 5 threads in a ring, each holds one lock and wants next
Fix each using: consistent ordering, trylock+backoff, and lock timeout respectively

CHALLENGE 2:
Build "Deadlock Detector" tool:
- Wraps all Lock objects in your program
- Tracks: which thread holds which lock, which thread waits for which lock
- Every 5 seconds: compute the wait-for graph
- Detect cycles in the graph using DFS
- When cycle found: print all threads in the deadlock cycle with stack traces

CHALLENGE 3:
Implement "Bankers Algorithm" for deadlock avoidance:
- N resources (each with a capacity), M threads (each with max needs)
- Before granting a request: check if resulting state is "safe"
- A state is safe if there exists an execution order where all threads complete
- Reject unsafe requests (thread must wait and retry)
- Test with 4 resources, 6 threads, random request patterns

CHALLENGE 4:
Demonstrate and fix Priority Inversion:
- 3 threads: HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW
- LOW thread holds a lock
- HIGH thread waits for that lock
- MEDIUM thread runs because it doesn't need the lock
- Show: HIGH is effectively blocked behind MEDIUM (inversion!)
- Fix using Priority Inheritance: LOW thread inherits HIGH's priority while holding lock

CHALLENGE 5:
Build "Livelock Demonstrator and Fixer":
- Two "polite" threads that always yield when they see the other waiting
- Show them cycling indefinitely (livelock)
- Fix 1: Random exponential backoff (jitter)
- Fix 2: Token-based ordering (one thread always yields first)
- Fix 3: Mediator thread that assigns access turns
- Measure: how many livelock cycles before resolution for each fix

CHALLENGE 6:
Create "Starvation-Free Reader-Writer Lock":
- Standard reader-writer lock: readers can starve writers or vice versa
- Implement "FIFO" reader-writer lock where requests are served in order:
  - Reader arrives while writer active: waits its turn
  - Writer arrives while readers active: waits its turn
  - NO new readers can jump ahead of a waiting writer
- Test: 8 readers + 3 writers, prove FIFO ordering

CHALLENGE 7:
Build "Production Deadlock Response System":
- Auto-detects deadlocks using a watchdog thread
- When deadlock detected: takes a thread dump (all stacks)
- Selects a "victim" thread (lowest priority or most recently started)
- Interrupts the victim: causes its lock.acquire() to raise DeadlockVictimError
- Victim catches error, releases all held locks, logs the incident, retries
- Test: deliberately create deadlocks and measure recovery time
```

- Subscribers: subscribe returns async generator
- Support: wildcard topics (e.g., 'events.*' matches 'events.user')
- Test: 5 publishers, 10 subscribers, 3 topics, 500 messages
- Guarantee: all subscribers receive all messages (no drops)

CHALLENGE 7:
Build "Async Distributed Cache" simulation:
- N cache node coroutines (simulate separate processes as coroutines)
- Consistent hashing: key → cache node assignment
- Read: check local node, then peers (async), then source
- Write: write to local + 2 replicas asynchronously
- Handle: node failure (timeout = node down), failover
- Test: 1000 read/write operations, measure hit rate and latency
```

sections.title: Thread Safety Patterns — Coding Challenges — Thread Safety Patterns
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
Implement all 7 thread safety patterns for the same use case
(a leaderboard with 1000 players):
a) Immutable snapshot approach
b) Thread confinement (each thread manages its own partition)
c) Locking (fine-grained per-player locks)
d) Copy-on-write (readers never block)
e) Thread-local (each thread has local cache, merges periodically)
f) Compare-and-swap (atomic score updates)
g) Actor model (single actor owns all scores)
Benchmark: throughput and latency for 10 readers + 5 writers

CHALLENGE 2:
Build "Thread-Safe Cache" with TTL using each of:
a) Global Lock (simple, baseline)
b) Read-Write Lock (readers don't block each other)
c) Striped Lock (16 locks, key % 16 selects lock)
d) Copy-on-write (readers always get snapshot)
Benchmark each under: read-heavy (90/10), balanced (50/50), write-heavy (10/90)

CHALLENGE 3:
Implement "Non-Blocking Stack" using Compare-And-Swap:
- push(item): atomic CAS to add to head
- pop(): atomic CAS to remove from head
- Retry if CAS fails (another thread changed head)
- Test: 8 threads pushing/popping 100K items
- Verify: no items lost or duplicated

CHALLENGE 4:
Create a "Thread-Safe Observer Pattern":
- Observable: can add/remove observers, notify all
- Observer: callback called on notification
- Thread-safety requirements:
  - Adding observer during notification is safe
  - Removing observer during notification is safe
  - Notification is non-blocking for sender
- Test: 5 observables, 10 observers, concurrent add/remove/notify

CHALLENGE 5:
Build "Persistent Data Structure" (immutable with history):
- ImmutableList: append returns NEW list, original unchanged
- Threads can hold references to old versions safely
- Implement structural sharing to minimize memory
- Test: 5 threads each holding a version reference,
  3 threads creating new versions concurrently
- Verify: no thread sees another thread's modifications

CHALLENGE 6:
Implement "Thread-Safe Singleton" with lazy initialization:
- Pattern A: Eager (initialize at module load)
- Pattern B: Double-Checked Locking (safe in Python?)
- Pattern C: Borg pattern (shared state, multiple instances)
- Pattern D: Module-level instance (Python's module lock)
- Test: 1000 threads all calling get_instance() simultaneously
- Verify: exactly ONE instance created

CHALLENGE 7:
Design "Thread-Safe Event Bus" for microservices:
- Topics: string names
- Events: immutable dataclasses
- Publishers: fire-and-forget (never block)
- Subscribers: async callbacks (run in background threads)
- Delivery guarantee: at-least-once
- Ordering guarantee: per-topic FIFO ordering
- Test: 10 publishers, 20 subscribers, 5 topics, 10000 events
```
